da-2026-ga-1.approach: Find the exact relation in the first pair (a pair of opposites), then pick the word that stands in the same relation to *Insolence*.

steps.title: Relation in the first pair
steps.body: **Verbosity** = using more words than needed; **Brevity** = using few words. They are **opposites** (antonyms).

steps.title: Apply it to Insolence
steps.body: **Insolence** = rude, disrespectful behaviour. Its opposite is **Respect** (courteous regard). So Verbosity : Brevity :: Insolence : **Respect**.

steps.title: Eliminate the other options
steps.body: *Innocence* is the opposite of **guilt**, *Solace* means **comfort**, and *Wealth* is the opposite of **poverty** — none of them is the opposite of insolence, so none keeps the antonym relation.

da-2026-ga-1.shortcut: Name the relation in one word ("opposite"), then ask "opposite of insolence?" — respect.

da-2026-ga-2.approach: Factor 70 into primes; the prime factors themselves are single digits, and no other split into three digits exists, so the digits are forced.

steps.title: Prime-factorise the product
steps.body: $$70 = 2 \times 5 \times 7$$

steps.title: The three digits are forced
steps.body: Each digit is from $1$ to $9$ (a $0$ would make the product $0$). Any other split into three factors needs a factor $\ge 10$: $70 = 1 \times 7 \times 10 = 1 \times 2 \times 35 = 1 \times 5 \times 14 = 1 \times 1 \times 70$, none valid. Combining two primes ($2 \times 5 = 10$, $2 \times 7 = 14$, $5 \times 7 = 35$) always gives a two-digit factor. So the digits are $\{2, 5, 7\}$ in some order (e.g. $257$, $725$).

steps.title: Sum of the digits
steps.body:
$$2 + 5 + 7 = 14$$
The sum is the same for every arrangement of the digits.

optionAnalysis.reason: 12 would need digits like $\{1, 4, 7\}$, whose product is $28$, not $70$.
Digits $2, 5, 7$: product $70$, sum $14$.
No set of three single digits with product $70$ sums to 16; the digits are forced to be $2, 5, 7$.
18 would need e.g. $1 + 7 + 10$, which uses the illegal "digit" 10.

da-2026-ga-2.shortcut: $70 = 2 \cdot 5 \cdot 7$ has exactly three prime factors, all single digits — add them: $14$.

da-2026-ga-3.approach: Each piece is one quarter (left, top, right, bottom) of the black background of the finished figure. Read off what each piece forces on the white silhouette, then eliminate the candidates that contradict any piece.

Pieces (each a full square, black only along one edge):

| Piece | Black edge | Feature it fixes |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | left | left half of a **round head**; a jagged lower-left edge |
| 2 | top | **round top** of the head (semicircular bite) |
| 3 | right | a long horizontal **beak** notch; upper-right edge of the body |
| 4 | bottom | two "peaks": the body ends in a **corner pointing down** |

steps.title: How the pieces combine
steps.body: Stacking the four squares, the black parts together form the black background; the region that is white in **all four** pieces is the white figure. So every white boundary in the answer must coincide with a black boundary printed in one of the pieces.

steps.title: Piece 3 forces a beak — Q is out
steps.body: Piece 3 has a long, thin white spike cut into its black band at mid-height, so the finished figure **must have a beak** pointing right. **Q** has no beak (its head ends in a blunt bump), so Q cannot be made.

steps.title: Piece 2 forces a round head — S is out
steps.body: Piece 2's black triangle has a smooth **semicircular** bite, so the top of the head must be a smooth round arc. **S** has a sharp V-shaped black notch in the top of its head (a pointed ear) — that would need a black wedge in piece 2, which is not there. S cannot be made.

steps.title: Piece 4 forces a pointed bottom — R is out
steps.body: Piece 4's top edge is a mountain profile: a small peak, a valley, then a big peak. The valley is the **lowest corner** of the tilted body and the big peak is its right corner. So the body must end in a downward-pointing corner. **R** has a flat horizontal bottom, which would need piece 4 to be black up to a straight horizontal line. R cannot be made.

steps.title: P matches every piece
steps.body: **P**: round head (pieces 1 and 2), beak to the right (piece 3), tilted rectangular body whose left corner and notch match piece 1, whose upper-right edge matches piece 3, and whose lowest corner matches the valley of piece 4. Every edge is accounted for, with no overlaps and no gaps.

optionAnalysis.reason: P's head, beak and pointed body coincide with the inner edges of all four pieces.
Q has no beak, but piece 3 cuts a beak-shaped notch into the right side.
R's body has a flat bottom, but piece 4 rises in two peaks with a valley — the body must end in a corner.
S has a V-notch in the top of its head, but piece 2 shows a smooth semicircular top.

da-2026-ga-3.shortcut: Look for the one distinctive feature in each piece (beak, round top, pointed bottom) and strike out every candidate missing one of them.
pitfalls: Comparing only the outline of the head and body and overlooking the beak notch in piece 3.
da-2026-ga-3.verification: Each wrong option fails a different piece (Q → piece 3, R → piece 4, S → piece 2), and P fails none — consistent with a single correct answer.

da-2026-ga-4.approach: Take $\log_{10}$ of both numbers: each becomes the same product $\log_{10} m \cdot \log_{10} n$, so the numbers are equal.

steps.title: Log of x
steps.body: $$\log_{10} x = \log_{10}\left(n^{\log_{10} m}\right) = \log_{10} m \cdot \log_{10} n$$

steps.title: Log of y
steps.body: $$\log_{10} y = \log_{10}\left(m^{\log_{10} n}\right) = \log_{10} n \cdot \log_{10} m$$

steps.title: Equal logs give equal numbers
steps.body: Multiplication is commutative, so $\log_{10} x = \log_{10} y$. Since $\log_{10}$ is one-to-one on positive reals, $x = y$ — whatever the values of $m > n > 0$.

optionAnalysis.reason: Assumes the larger base $m$ makes a difference; the logs of $x$ and $y$ are identical.
Same error in the other direction; $x$ and $y$ are always equal.
Would require $x = \log_{10} x$, which has no solution among positive reals.

da-2026-ga-4.shortcut: Remember the identity $a^{\log b} = b^{\log a}$ (any fixed base).
pitfalls: Plugging in one example and misreading rounding as an inequality.

da-2026-ga-5.approach: The sentence is a past counterfactual (third conditional: *had been … would have*). Such a sentence implies that the condition did **not** happen in reality.

steps.title: Identify the structure
steps.body: "If his latest movie **had been** a commercial success, the actor **would have made** enough money…" — *if + past perfect … would have + past participle* is the **third conditional**, used for imagined situations in the past that did not occur.

steps.title: What it implies
steps.body: The speaker imagines success that did not happen. So, in reality, **his latest movie was not a commercial success**, and therefore he did not make that money from it.

steps.title: Check each statement
steps.body: Only (D) follows. (B) and (C) contradict the implication; (A) talks about the future, about which the sentence says nothing certain.

answer.value: **His latest movie was not commercially successful** — option (D)

optionAnalysis.reason: The sentence implies he did *not* make the money; nothing makes his sponsoring the next movie certain.
Contradicts the counterfactual *had been*: the success did not happen.
"Would have made" means he did not actually make enough money from it.
A third conditional states the opposite of reality: the movie was not a commercial success.

da-2026-ga-5.shortcut: *had + V3 … would have + V3* ⇒ negate both clauses to get the real facts.
pitfalls: Reading the conditional as a statement of fact and choosing (B).
da-2026-ga-5.verification: Rephrase: "The movie was not a success, so the actor did not make enough money" — this is exactly what the original sentence conveys.

da-2026-ga-6.approach: Use fixed preposition collocations: *at* a point location (the door), *of* for belonging (door of the cabin), *for* a duration (for the night).

steps.title: First blank: parted ___ the door
steps.body: A meeting point is a place → **at** the door ("we parted at the station / at the gate").

steps.title: Second blank: the door ___ the cabin
steps.body: The door belongs to the cabin → **of** ("the door of the cabin").

steps.title: Third blank: rented ___ the night
steps.body: A period of time for which something is rented → **for** ("rented for the night").

optionAnalysis.reason: "parted **at** the door **of** the cabin … rented **for** the night" — every collocation is standard.
"parted for the door" means leaving towards it, and "rented of the night" is ungrammatical.
"parted of the door" and "door for the cabin" are both wrong.
"parted in the door" is wrong: one stands *at* (not *in*) a door.

da-2026-ga-6.shortcut: The third blank alone settles it: only (A) and (D) give "for the night", and "in the door" is wrong.
pitfalls: Choosing *in* the door — *in the doorway* is possible, but *in the door* is not idiomatic here.
da-2026-ga-6.verification: Read the full sentence: "My friend and I parted at the door of the cabin that I had rented for the night." It is natural English.

da-2026-ga-7.approach: Sort the five numbers. The median fixes the middle one, a single mode of 20 forces exactly the two largest to be 20, and the mean fixes the sum of the remaining two — then rule out the case that creates a second mode.

steps.title: Set up the sorted list
steps.body:
Let $a \le b \le c \le d \le e$, all in $[0, 20]$. Median $= c = 18$. Mean $= 12$ gives
$$a + b + c + d + e = 5 \times 12 = 60.$$

steps.title: Placing the mode 20
steps.body: A mode must occur at least twice. Since $c = 18 < 20$, the value 20 can only be $d$ or $e$, so it occurs **at most twice** — hence exactly twice: $d = e = 20$.

scene.caption: 20 can only sit in the two top slots

steps.title: Keep the mode single
steps.body: $(1, 1)$ gives $\{1, 1, 18, 20, 20\}$: both 1 and 20 occur twice — two modes, not allowed. $(0, 2)$ gives $\{0, 2, 18, 20, 20\}$: mean $\frac{0+2+18+20+20}{5} = \frac{60}{5} = 12$, median $18$, only mode $20$. Exactly **one** multiset works.

optionAnalysis.reason: $\{0, 2, 18, 20, 20\}$ satisfies all three conditions, so at least one way exists.
Only $(a, b) = (0, 2)$ survives; $(1, 1)$ creates a second mode.
Counts $\{1, 1, 18, 20, 20\}$ too, ignoring that the mode must be single.
Over-counts, e.g. by letting 20 appear three times — impossible because the median is 18.

pitfalls: Trying $20$ three times — that would make the median 20.

da-2026-ga-8.approach: Three games eliminate three players, so the knock-out structure is fixed: the winner of each game plays the next. Split on which same-class pair played the first game and test conditions (i)–(iii).
da-2026-ga-8.given:
| Student | Class | Gender |
|---|---|---|
| Rishi | 5 | boy |
| Swathi | 5 | girl |
| Pavan | 4 | boy |
| Tanvi | 4 | girl |

steps.title: Structure of the games
steps.body: Each game has one loser, who then stops playing, so 3 games eliminate 3 players and exactly **one student never loses**. Game 1 is between two students of the **same class**; games 2 and 3 must be between **different classes** (condition (i)). Condition (ii): Class 5 wins at least 2 of the 3 games.

steps.title: Case: game 1 is Pavan vs Tanvi — impossible
steps.body: Class 4 wins game 1, so Class 5 must win games 2 and 3. Game 2 (cross-class) is the Class-4 winner vs Rishi or Swathi, and the Class-5 player wins. Then the only two players left are Rishi and Swathi — both Class 5 — so game 3 would be same-class, violating (i). **Rejected.**

scene.caption: Game 1 must be Rishi vs Swathi

steps.title: Game 1 is Rishi vs Swathi; the winner must win game 2
steps.body: Call the winner $W$ (Class 5). Game 2 must be cross-class, so it is $W$ vs Pavan or Tanvi. If the Class-4 player won game 2, game 3 would be Pavan vs Tanvi (same class) ✗. So **$W$ wins game 2**, and game 3 is $W$ vs the other Class-4 student.

steps.title: Use the boys/girls count
steps.body: If $W$ = Swathi (girl), girls already have 2 wins (games 1, 2) ✗ (girls won only one). So $W$ = **Rishi**, who has won 2 games — exactly the boys' total. Hence game 3 is won by a **girl** from Class 4: **Tanvi**. So game 2 was Rishi vs Pavan, game 3 Rishi vs Tanvi.

steps.title: Check all conditions
steps.body: Wins: Rishi 2 (Class 5, boy), Tanvi 1 (Class 4, girl). (i) only game 1 was same-class ✓; (ii) Class 5: 2 > Class 4: 1 ✓; (iii) boys 2, girls 1 ✓. Losers: Swathi, Pavan, Rishi — the student who never lost is **Tanvi**.

scene.caption: Swathi, Pavan and Rishi each lost once; Tanvi never lost

optionAnalysis.reason: Pavan loses game 2 to Rishi.
Rishi wins two games but loses the third to Tanvi (otherwise boys would win 3).
Swathi loses game 1; if she had won it, girls would have at least 2 wins.
Tanvi wins the last game and plays no other game, so she never loses.

da-2026-ga-8.shortcut: Game 1 must be Class 5 vs Class 5 (else games 2–3 can't both be cross-class with Class 5 winning). Its winner must win game 2, and with boys = 2 wins the winner is Rishi, who then loses game 3 to a girl → Tanvi.
pitfalls: Forgetting that the last two players must also be from different classes.
Assuming the student who never lost must be the one who won the most games.
da-2026-ga-8.verification: Only one schedule satisfies all three conditions: Rishi > Swathi, Rishi > Pavan, Tanvi > Rishi.

steps.title: Bound the numbers
steps.body:
Let the consecutive numbers be $n$ and $n+1$. $XYP$ has three digits, so
$$n^2 + (n+1)^2 = 2n^2 + 2n + 1 \le 999.$$
$n = 21$: $2(441) + 42 + 1 = 925$ ✓; $n = 22$: $2(484) + 44 + 1 = 1013$ ✗. So $10 \le n \le 21$ and both numbers lie in $10$–$22$.

steps.title: Distinct tens digits
steps.body: $P$ and $R$ are the tens digits of $PQ$ and $RS$, and all six letters are distinct, so $P \ne R$. Two consecutive numbers have different tens digits only when they straddle a multiple of 10: within $10$–$22$ that is **19 and 20**.

steps.title: Check distinctness
steps.body: $P, Q, R, S, X, Y = 1, 9, 2, 0, 7, 6$ — all different ✓. So $Y = 6$.

optionAnalysis.reason: 4 would be $Y$ only for a sum like $X4P$; e.g. $221 = 10^2 + 11^2$ has middle digit 2, and no valid pair gives 4.
5 is the units digit of $265 = 11^2 + 12^2$, a pair with equal tens digits (not allowed).
$19^2 + 20^2 = 761$, so $Y = 6$ with all six digits distinct.
7 is $X$ (the hundreds digit of 761), not $Y$.

da-2026-ga-9.shortcut: Distinct tens digits ⇒ the pair crosses a decade ⇒ 19, 20 (the next crossing, 29/30, is far above 999) ⇒ $761$ ⇒ $Y = 6$.

da-2026-ga-10.approach: Split the shaded region along $OQ$ into two congruent triangles $OPQ$ and $ORQ$. The inscribed angle gives $\angle POR = 90^\circ$, hence $\angle POQ = 135^\circ$, and each triangle's area is $\tfrac12 r^2 \sin 135^\circ$.
da-2026-ga-10.given: Radius $r = 10$ cm, $PQ = RQ$, $\angle PQR = 45^\circ$; shaded region $PQRO$ (arrowhead shape with $O$ inside triangle $PQR$).

steps.title: Central angle POR
steps.body:
$\angle PQR = 45^\circ$ is inscribed and subtends arc $PR$ (the one not containing $Q$), so the central angle on the same arc is
$$\angle POR = 2 \times 45^\circ = 90^\circ.$$

steps.title: Angles POQ and ROQ
steps.body:
$PQ = RQ$ makes the figure symmetric about $OQ$, so $\angle POQ = \angle ROQ$. The three angles around $O$ add to $360^\circ$:
$$\angle POQ = \frac{360^\circ - 90^\circ}{2} = \frac{270^\circ}{2} = 135^\circ.$$

steps.title: Area of the shaded region
steps.body:
$PQRO = \triangle OPQ + \triangle ORQ$, each with two sides equal to the radius:
$$\text{Area} = 2 \times \tfrac12 \times 10 \times 10 \times \sin 135^\circ = 100 \times \frac{\sqrt2}{2} = 50\sqrt2 \approx 70.7 \text{ cm}^2.$$

optionAnalysis.reason: 50 is the area of triangle $POR$ ($\tfrac12 \times 10 \times 10$), the white notch — not the shaded part.
$25\sqrt2$ is the area of only one of the two triangles $OPQ$, $ORQ$.
$2 \times \tfrac12 \times 10^2 \sin 135^\circ = 50\sqrt2$.
Results from using $\sin 90^\circ$ instead of $\sin 135^\circ$, i.e. treating $\angle POQ$ as a right angle.

Using the reflex angle $270^\circ$ instead of splitting it into two $135^\circ$ angles.

da-2026-da-1.approach: Principal components are eigenvectors of the (symmetric) covariance matrix, and PCA takes them mutually orthogonal — so any two distinct components, including the 1st and 10th, are at $90^\circ$.

steps.title: What the principal components are
steps.body: PCA computes the covariance matrix $\Sigma = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i (x_i - \bar x)(x_i - \bar x)^T$ ($100 \times 100$) and takes its eigenvectors in decreasing order of eigenvalue. Keeping 10 dimensions means keeping the top 10 eigenvectors $u_1, \ldots, u_{10}$.

steps.title: They are orthonormal
steps.body: $\Sigma$ is symmetric, so by the spectral theorem its eigenvectors can be chosen orthonormal (and PCA does so: each new component maximises variance **subject to being orthogonal** to the earlier ones). Hence $u_1^T u_{10} = 0$.

steps.title: Angle
steps.body:
$$\cos\theta = \frac{u_1^T u_{10}}{\lVert u_1\rVert\,\lVert u_{10}\rVert} = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \theta = 90^\circ.$$
The reduction from 100 to 10 dimensions and the classification task do not change this.

optionAnalysis.reason: $0^\circ$ would mean the two components are the same direction — distinct components are never parallel.
Principal components are orthogonal eigenvectors of the symmetric covariance matrix.
An obtuse angle would need $u_1^T u_{10} < 0$, but the dot product is exactly 0.
An acute angle would need $u_1^T u_{10} > 0$; components are uncorrelated directions with zero dot product.

da-2026-da-1.shortcut: Any two different principal components ⇒ orthogonal ⇒ $90^\circ$.
pitfalls: Thinking the angle depends on how many components are kept or on their variance ranks.
da-2026-da-1.verification: In 2-D data, PC1 is the long axis of the data ellipse and PC2 its short axis — perpendicular, as for every pair of components.

da-2026-da-2.approach: LOOCV is run only on the data available for model selection (the 900 non-test samples), and it makes one split per sample: each sample is the validation set once.

steps.title: Data available for model selection
steps.body:
Of the $1000$ samples, the first $100$ are reserved for testing and must not be touched during model selection. That leaves
$$1000 - 100 = 900$$
samples for training + validation.

steps.title: Splits in LOOCV
steps.body: Leave-one-out is $k$-fold cross-validation with $k = $ number of samples: each split trains on $899$ samples and validates on the $1$ left out. With $900$ samples there are **900** splits.

steps.title: Ignore the distractors
steps.body: The number of classes (10) and the input dimension (512) do not affect how many splits are made.

optionAnalysis.reason: 10 is the number of classes, irrelevant to the number of LOOCV folds.
512 is the feature dimension, irrelevant to the folds.
One split per non-test sample: $1000 - 100 = 900$.
Counts the 100 test samples too, which would leak test data into model selection.

da-2026-da-2.shortcut: LOOCV folds $=$ number of samples used for model selection $= 900$.
pitfalls: Including the test set in cross-validation (answer 1000).
da-2026-da-2.verification: Each of the 900 samples is held out exactly once, so $900$ train/validate runs are needed.

da-2026-da-3.approach: Uninformed (blind) search uses only the problem definition; informed search uses a heuristic estimate $h(n)$ of the remaining cost. A* uses $f(n) = g(n) + h(n)$, so it is the informed one.

steps.title: Uninformed strategies
steps.body: **BFS**, **DFS** and **depth-limited search** choose the next node only from the structure of the search tree (depth, order of generation). They use no estimate of the distance to the goal.

steps.title: A* is informed
steps.body: **A\*** expands the node with the smallest $f(n) = g(n) + h(n)$, where $h(n)$ is a **heuristic** estimate of the cost from $n$ to the goal. Using $h$ makes it an informed (heuristic) search.

steps.title: Classify the options
steps.body:
| Option | Uses a heuristic $h(n)$? | Type |
|---|---|---|
| BFS | no | uninformed |
| DFS | no | uninformed |
| A* | yes, $f = g + h$ | **informed** |
| Depth-limited | no (only a depth cut-off) | uninformed |

So A* is the one that is **not** uninformed.

optionAnalysis.reason: BFS explores level by level with no heuristic — uninformed.
DFS follows the deepest node first with no heuristic — uninformed.
A* uses the heuristic $h(n)$ in $f(n) = g(n) + h(n)$ — informed search.
Depth-limited search is DFS with a depth cut-off — still uninformed.

da-2026-da-3.shortcut: Look for the algorithm that needs a heuristic $h(n)$: A* (also greedy best-first) is informed.
pitfalls: Thinking depth-limited search is informed because it uses a depth bound — the bound is not a goal-distance estimate.
da-2026-da-3.verification: Standard classification (Russell & Norvig): uninformed = BFS, uniform-cost, DFS, depth-limited, iterative deepening, bidirectional; informed = greedy best-first, A*.
